rationale: A wins because it knows the difference between a sharp angle and a dressed-up assumption. "Whoop's new blood-pressure number isn't a medical reading — and needs a cuff to even start" is grounded, uncomfortable, and pitchable once the proof is nailed down. B has useful bones, but "AFib Detection on Your Wrist Is Now a Premium Feature — and That's a Health Equity Story" jumps from paywall to equity without the population, pricing, or access evidence needed to carry that word.
gaps_in_A: "screenless band" is not in the supplied update; it may be true Whoop context, but the set should flag it as a proof item, not smuggle it into the hook.
"the wearable was supposed to replace" overstates the cuff-calibration fact; the update says one-time calibration, not that users still need a cuff for ongoing readings.
"health features are increasingly paywalled" needs category evidence; A admits the trend framing needs more than one company, but the angle still leans on that broader claim before proving it.
It leaves the regulatory/wellness boundary underdeveloped; "non-medical 'wellness' estimate, not a diagnostic" could support a medtech-regulatory angle if FDA-path proof exists.
gaps_in_B: "Health Equity Story" is too big for the supplied facts; a premium tier creates an access question, not a health-equity story without pricing, affected populations, or disparity evidence.
"That Word Choice Is Doing Legal Work" and "deliberate regulatory positioning move" state intent and legal strategy the update does not prove.
"Apple Watch Has Had It for Years" names a competitor and timeline not supplied; that belongs in proof-needed, not the headline.
"The $3.6 Billion Wearable That Still Needs a Blood Pressure Cuff" uses valuation as cheap contrast without a financial thesis; it hints at investor/business significance the update does not support.
